young.html: In 1643 the Parliament of England passed a law that every book had to be read and approved by an official, called a licenser, before it could be printed. The poet John Milton thought this was a terrible idea, and in 1644 he wrote a speech-in-print called Areopagitica to argue against it.

Milton said that killing a good book is almost as bad as killing a person, because a book holds the best thoughts of a mind. He also said that people become good by meeting bad ideas and choosing the right ones, not by being kept from ever seeing them. Truth, he said, is strong: in a fair fight, it wins.

young.html: Milton also wrote short poems. When he went blind, he wrote a sonnet, a poem of 14 lines, asking how he could still serve God without his sight. It ends with a famous line: They also serve who only stand and wait. He meant that being patient and faithful is a kind of service too.

Fair fight for ideas. Pick a friendly question, like “Are cats or dogs better pets?” One person gives the best reasons for one side, the other for the other side. Then switch sides! Talk about it: did hearing both sides help you think? This is what Milton meant by letting ideas meet in a free and open encounter.

full.html: John Milton (1608–1674) is best known for Paradise Lost (its own rung). This rung gathers the rest of the Milton volume: his early English poems, the speech Areopagitica (1644) and the drama Samson Agonistes (1671). In June 1643 Parliament, at war with King Charles I, ordered that no book be printed without a licenser's approval. Milton, whose own writings on divorce had been printed without a license and attacked, answered with Areopagitica, written as if it were a speech to Parliament. The title recalls the Areopagus, the ancient council of Athens, and a speech of the same kind by the Greek orator Isocrates.

items: Where licensing came from. Milton argues that the ancient Greeks and Romans punished only certain books after they appeared, and that licensing before printing was a recent invention of the church courts and the Inquisition. This is his history and his framing.
Reading tests virtue. Good and evil grow up together in this world. A person becomes wise by knowing evil and choosing good.
It won't work. Evil ideas spread by conversation, music and many other ways; licensers are fallible and overworked.
It harms learning and truth. It insults scholars and slows the search for truth, which grows through open debate.

full.text: …as good almost kill a man as kill a good book. Who kills a man kills a reasonable creature, God's image; but he who destroys a good book, kills reason itself, kills the image of God, as it were in the eye.

full.html: The limits of Milton's case. Milton did not ask that every book go unpunished. He accepted that a book shown to be harmful could be burned and its author punished after printing, and he excluded Roman Catholic worship and what he called open superstition from the toleration he wanted. Historians also note that he later served for a time as an official licenser of a government newsbook.

The early poems include the ode On the Morning of Christ's Nativity (1629), the paired poems L'Allegro and Il Penseroso (the cheerful man and the thoughtful man), the masque Comus (1634), a play with music about a young lady who resists a sorcerer, and Lycidas (1637), an elegy for a drowned college friend. His sonnets include the one on his blindness:

full.text:
Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
And post o're Land and Ocean without rest:

full.html: Samson Agonistes (“Samson the champion”) is a tragedy in the Greek form, not meant for the stage. Samson, blind and a prisoner of the Philistines, is visited by his father, by Dalila, and by a boastful giant, and slowly recovers his faith. At a festival he pulls down the Philistines' temple, dying himself; the play reports this through a messenger, as Greek tragedies did. Many readers have heard Milton's own blindness and defeat in Samson's laments.

deep.html: Areopagitica changed nothing at first: licensing went on, and the speech was little noticed. Pre-publication licensing in England finally lapsed in 1695 for practical and political reasons. In the 18th century, writers on liberty of the press in Britain and America quoted Milton often, and his image of truth and falsehood grappling in open encounter is echoed in later arguments for free discussion, including John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859), later on this ladder.

Milton's critics in his day argued that a society at war had to stop books that stirred up rebellion or attacked religion, and that ordinary readers needed protection from error. Milton answered that the cure was more argument, not less. Thinkers ever since have debated where the line falls, and Milton himself drew lines that most later defenders of free expression would not.

items: Does truth always win in a free and open encounter? What does it need in order to win?
Should any books be kept from children? From adults? Who should decide?
Is it better to stop harmful words before they are spoken or to answer them afterward?

questions: Milton said a good book holds “the image of God” in a mind. What book would you save from a fire? Why?
Can you become good without ever being tempted? What did Milton think?
What is a time hearing the other side of an argument changed your mind?
Milton wanted freedom to print, but not for everyone. Is that fair? Why do you think he drew the line where he did?
“They also serve who only stand and wait.” When is waiting a way of helping?
